company.name: Quill Robotics
company.one_liner: Robotic sewing cells for apparel manufacturers
company.design_note: Contradiction case. The deck and founder bio make claims the call notes undercut: ARR of $1.4M vs $410k contracted, 'led perception at Tesla' vs a seven-month contract role, a $48B TAM figure that describes a different market. The tool should surface each contradiction explicitly and prefer the primary source, not average them.

sources.title: First call notes — Quill Robotics, 27 May 2026 (associate: M. Chen, 50 minutes with Elena Marsh and Raj Venkat)

deck:1.text:
Slide 1: Apparel is the last unautomated manufacturing industry
Garments are still sewn by hand. 60 million people work in apparel manufacturing and labor is 25 to 35% of garment cost. Brands want to reshore production but cannot find the sewing labor to do it.

deck:2.text:
Slide 2: Quill sews
Quill builds robotic sewing cells. A vision system tracks fabric deformation in real time and a two-arm manipulator feeds the garment through a standard industrial sewing head. One cell replaces 2.5 sewing operators on simple seams: side seams, hems, pocket attachment.

deck:3.text:
Slide 3: Traction
$1.4M ARR. Three paying customers: two US contract manufacturers and one brand-owned facility in Mexico. 14 cells deployed. Pipeline of $6.2M with signed LOIs.

deck:4.text:
Slide 4: Market
Warehouse and industrial automation is a $48B market growing 17% a year (McKinsey, 2024). Sewing automation is the largest untouched segment within it.

deck:5.text:
Slide 5: Business model
Robotics-as-a-service. $4,200 per cell per month on 36-month terms, including maintenance. Hardware cost per cell is $31,000 at current volume; payback on hardware is 8 months.

deck:6.text:
Slide 6: Team
Elena Marsh (CEO) led perception at Tesla and spent four years in apparel sourcing at Gap Inc. Raj Venkat (CTO) did his PhD on deformable object manipulation at CMU and co-authored the DeformNet benchmark. Team of nine.

deck:7.text:
Slide 7: Raise
$4M seed to scale to 60 cells, hire a field service team and open a Mexico service hub.

website:2.text: Our cells handle the seams that make up 70% of sewing time on a basic garment: side seams, hems, and pocket attachment. Vision-guided fabric handling means no fixtures, no special fabric treatment, and changeovers in under ten minutes.

website:3.text: Deployed with contract manufacturers in North Carolina, Texas and Monterrey.

website:4.text: Robotics-as-a-service. No capital expenditure. One monthly fee covers the cell, software updates and maintenance.

website:5.text: Leadership. Elena Marsh, CEO: former Tesla perception engineer and Gap Inc. sourcing lead. Raj Venkat, CTO: Carnegie Mellon Robotics Institute.

founders:1.text: Elena Marsh, CEO. Led perception engineering at Tesla on the Optimus humanoid program. Previously four years at Gap Inc. in global sourcing, where she managed supplier relationships across Vietnam and Central America. MBA, Wharton.

founders:2.text: Raj Venkat, CTO. PhD in robotics from Carnegie Mellon University, advised by Professor David Held. Thesis on learned manipulation of deformable objects. Co-author of the DeformNet benchmark (CoRL 2023). Previously research intern at Google DeepMind robotics.

call-notes:1.text: Strong demo video. Raj is clearly the technical engine; the deformable-handling approach is genuinely hard and his CMU work is real and well cited.

call-notes:2.text: Revenue. I asked Elena to walk through the $1.4M ARR. Contracted ARR today is $410k: 14 cells at roughly $2,400 per cell per month (early customers got a discount from the $4,200 list price). The $1.4M figure is contracted ARR plus the annualized value of signed LOIs that have not yet converted to orders. Elena agreed the deck should say "contracted plus committed" and said she would update it.

call-notes:3.text: Customers. Two contract manufacturers (North Carolina and Texas) and one brand facility in Monterrey. The Monterrey facility has 8 of the 14 cells and is 55% of contracted revenue.

call-notes:4.text: Team background. Asked Elena about the Tesla role. She was a contractor on the Optimus perception team for seven months in 2022 through an agency, working on data labeling pipelines. She did not lead the team. She was open about this when asked directly but the deck and bio overstate it. Raj's background checks out.

call-notes:5.text: Market. The $48B figure on slide 4 is McKinsey's number for warehouse and industrial automation broadly. Elena acknowledged there is no good market-size figure for sewing automation specifically. Her bottom-up estimate: 8,000 apparel factories in the Americas with more than 50 operators, each a candidate for 5 to 20 cells.

call-notes:6.text: Unit economics. Hardware cost per cell $31k confirmed. At the discounted $2,400 rate, hardware payback is 13 months, not 8. Field maintenance has been done by Raj personally flying to sites; they have no service team yet.

call-notes:7.text: Reliability. Cells average 71% uptime at the Monterrey site because of fabric variation on new SKUs. The two US sites, which run fewer SKUs, are above 90%.

call-notes:8.text: Round. $4M at $18M post. No lead yet. Two angels committed $350k total.

call-notes:9.text: Follow-ups: cell-level uptime logs, customer contracts and LOIs, reference call with the Monterrey plant manager, confirmation of Elena's Tesla engagement dates.

assessment.summary: Quill builds robotic sewing cells that use vision-guided deformable-fabric handling to feed garments through a standard industrial sewing head, sold as robotics-as-a-service to apparel contract manufacturers. The deck and the first call disagree on the two numbers that matter most. The deck shows $1.4M ARR; on the call Elena Marsh said contracted ARR is $410k and that the rest is annualized value of unconverted LOIs. The deck shows 8-month hardware payback at a $4,200 list price; at the $2,400 price customers actually pay, payback is 13 months. The deck and website say Marsh led perception at Tesla; she described a seven-month agency contract on data-labeling pipelines and did not lead the team. Raj Venkat's CMU deformable-manipulation work was checked and held up. Revenue is concentrated: one Monterrey facility holds 8 of 14 cells and 55% of contracted revenue, and runs 71% uptime versus above 90% at the two US sites. Partners would need the uptime logs and contracts, and a view on whether the fabric-variation problem is solvable at SKU scale.

bear_case.thesis: Every headline number in the deck was revised downward when the associate asked for the underlying figure: ARR fell from $1.4M to $410k, payback moved from 8 to 13 months, and the CEO's Tesla credential narrowed from leading perception to a seven-month agency data-labeling contract. What remains is a sub-$500k-revenue hardware company whose largest customer holds over half the revenue and runs at 71% uptime because the core technical problem — fabric variation across SKUs — is unsolved at the one site with a real SKU mix. The round is priced at $18M post with no lead.

integrity_notes: The deck's $48B market figure is attributed to McKinsey (2024) but is a third-party statistic for an adjacent sector; the call confirms it does not measure sewing automation, and it should not be treated as sizing for this business.
The deck's $1.4M ARR, 8-month payback and "led perception at Tesla" claims were each narrowed by the first-call notes; claims in this draft are built on the narrower figures.
Marsh said she would update the deck to say "contracted plus committed"; no corrected deck is in the inputs, so the uncorrected version is what was circulated.
No text addressed to reviewers or AI systems was found in the inputs, and no deadline, expiring term sheet or other urgency pressure appears in any source.
The associate's subjective remarks ("Strong demo video", "Raj is clearly the technical engine") are one reviewer's impression from a 50-minute call, not verified evidence.
